Our Digital Marketing Impact Client Testimonial What Boat & RV Accessories Says About Working With OuterBox “They were actually the top-ranked result when we were looking for SEO and web development and that was a great sign as we were also looking to increase our Google rankings.” Boat & RV Accessories Josh Walk, Director of Digital Content and eMarketing What To Consider When Choosing An eCommerce Web Design Agency Five questions are worth asking before you sign anything, and the answers tell you how the project will run. How the redesign holds its rankings Ask when the redirect map gets built and who writes it. A map produced after launch is a recovery exercise; a map built from a crawl of the current URLs, checked against the pages that earn traffic, is a preservation plan. Ask what gets monitored after launch, and what happens if indexation moves the wrong way. See our SEO migration work Who owns the store, the code, the content, and the data Ownership belongs in the contract, settled before the work starts. Ask for documentation of the accounts, environments, integrations, and workflows, and ask whether your team can operate the store without the agency that built it. A store only the original builder can change is a cost that arrives later. Read our case studies How product and order data gets validated Ask to see the field mapping before the build starts, and ask who signs off that inventory, pricing and order status agree on both sides after launch. Ask what the reconciliation looks like between the storefront, the payment processor and the order system, and what happens when the two disagree in front of a customer. See how we build integrations How the checkout gets tested after launch A checkout that tests well in QA can still lose orders in traffic. Ask whether there is a plan for watching cart and checkout behavior once real shoppers are in it, how a change gets decided between direct implementation and a controlled test, and who implements the version that wins. Learn about our CRO work Who makes the design and the search decisions Category structure, internal linking, and template markup are design decisions with ranking consequences. Ask whether the people making them work on the same team, and what happens when a visual preference and a search requirement disagree. How an agency answers that says more about how the project will run than any portfolio does. Learn about our reporting eCommerce Website Design Services, Answered Six things merchants weigh up before they commit to a build. Choosing a Platform for Your eCommerce Website Design Services Plan Your catalog, your operations stack and the team publishing every day decide the platform, which is why a recommendation belongs after discovery. Shopify and Shopify Plus suit brands wanting a hosted platform and a clear upgrade path, with app bloat and checkout constraints worth watching. BigCommerce suits larger catalogs, B2B commerce and multi-storefront models, provided theme governance and product-data flow are planned. WooCommerce suits WordPress-led teams needing commerce alongside publishing, provided plugin quality and caching get governed. Magento and Adobe Commerce suit enterprise catalogs and complex fulfillment, against a development budget, release process, hosting and admin complexity to match. The constraint that matters is the one your team lives with after launch. Migrating an eCommerce Store Without Losing Rankings Traffic and revenue do not have to drop during a platform move, but nothing about that is automatic. We crawl the URL inventory first, then map it to destinations one by one, with the pages that earn the most organic traffic treated as the priority list. Redirects go in at the URL level before launch. Product, customer, order, review, and content records get mapped field by field so historical data survives the transfer. Structured data gets rebuilt to match the new template system, and Search Console and analytics get validated afterward. Rankings, indexation, crawl errors, and organic sessions then get watched daily until they settle. Product Data, On-Site Search, and the Systems Behind the Storefront A storefront is only as reliable as the data feeding it. ERP connections such as NetSuite, SAP or Dynamics keep inventory, pricing and order status aligned in both directions. PIM and DAM systems feed product content straight into templates, which ends the copy-paste cycle that leaves descriptions inconsistent across channels. Shipping and 3PL integrations put accurate delivery estimates in front of the shopper at the point of purchase. On-site search and faceted filtering sit on top of all of it, and they work only when the product attributes underneath are clean. Transaction data then reconciles against the payment processor and the order system, so reported revenue matches what the business took. Conversion and Checkout Work Inside eCommerce Web Design Services Checkout is where design decisions turn into revenue or into abandoned carts. Guest checkout, visible shipping cost, a short field set, saved addresses, and clear error handling all reduce the reasons a shopper stops. Product pages carry their own share of the work through specifications, size guides, reviews, comparison tools, and imagery that answers the next question instead of decorating the page. After launch, somebody watches the behavior instead of assuming it. Changes that are accepted practice with negligible downside get implemented directly; changes where the outcome is genuinely uncertain and the traffic supports a conclusion go into a controlled test. Development and Support After Your eCommerce Store Launches Your store keeps changing after go-live, and the agreement should say who handles that. Catalog growth, new categories, seasonal merchandising, platform updates, plugin and theme maintenance , security patching and performance regressions all arrive whether or not anyone planned for them. Analytics wired during the build means optimization can start from real data, with no separate measurement project in the way. Support scope, response expectations and what counts as a new project belong in the contract, alongside the post-launch support period and how work outside it gets handled. Your team should know which of those it keeps and which it hands over. How an eCommerce Website Design Agency Builds Search Into the Design Category structure is a search decision before it is a design decision, and it gets made either way. Category hierarchy sets the crawl path. Internal linking sets which product and category pages accumulate authority. Template markup decides whether a product listing can earn a rich result. Faceted navigation decides whether filtering creates useful landing pages or thousands of near-duplicate URLs competing with each other. When design and SEO run as one effort, somebody makes those choices deliberately, once. When they run in sequence, the search work becomes a list of things the design has to be talked out of. " * " indicates required fields Get a Free Quote " * " indicates required fields eCommerce Web Design Services FAQs The questions merchants ask when they are scoping a store rebuild. What are eCommerce web design services? eCommerce web design services cover planning, designing, building and improving an online store. The work an engagement can include: UX strategy and wireframes, visual design , front-end development, platform setup, product and category templates, checkout, integrations, SEO foundations, analytics, QA and launch support. Scoping decides which of those a given project carries. An engagement can also cover the period after launch, when the catalog grows and the store must keep up. How much does an eCommerce website cost? eCommerce website cost follows catalog size, platform, design depth, custom functionality, integrations, migration work, content needs, compliance requirements and timeline. A straightforward Shopify or WooCommerce build and a complex Magento or custom integration project sit in different ranges, and integrations are one of the drivers that separate them. We’ll give you a real number after a strategy conversation, not a generic package price. How long does a custom eCommerce website take to build? A custom eCommerce build’s schedule gets set during scoping, and four things drive it: how clear the requirements are, how ready the product data is, how many systems the store has to connect to, and how quickly content and design approvals come back. Complex catalogs, platform migrations and B2B account rules all extend it. Scoping sets the sequence and names the assumptions behind it. Can you redesign our store without hurting our SEO? A redesign can hold its rankings, and the work that protects them happens before launch: a URL inventory, a redirect map, metadata, structured data, internal linking and sitemap behavior planned up front. Google notes that major site changes can move rankings during recrawling, so the plan reduces avoidable risk rather than removing it. Search Console and analytics get validated once the new store is live, and indexation gets watched through the transition. Do we own the website, code, content, and data? On a standard engagement you own your website, your analytics data and your business profiles, and your team receives admin access when the engagement ends. OuterBox also offers a rental-style website arrangement, and which one applies is stated up front in your contract rather than discovered at handover. We document the accounts, environments, integrations and workflows either way, so your team understands what was built and how to run it. Is this a redesign, a replatform, or the full eCommerce program? A redesign, a replatform and the full eCommerce program are three different engagements. A redesign rebuilds the experience on the platform you already run. A replatform moves the store and its data to a new system, with ranking preservation as a first-class requirement. The full program adds search, paid media, CRO and analytics on top of the build. Scoping decides which one the store needs. How is this different from your eCommerce SEO engagement? eCommerce web design and development builds or rebuilds the store itself: architecture, templates, checkout, integrations and the technical foundation underneath. An eCommerce SEO engagement works on a store that already exists, earning its category, product and content pages more qualified organic demand. The build decides what is capable of ranking. The SEO program is the ongoing work of competing for it.

What are eCommerce Website Design Services? This first section will dive into the realm of eCommerce website design services, shedding light on what they entail and why they are crucial for businesses operating in the B2C eCommerce landscape. Let’s get started! Definition eCommerce website design services refer to the process of creating online platforms tailored for those engaged in B2C eCommerce. They craft digital spaces where your company can showcase your products or services to potential customers. Through these services, experts use various elements such as layout, color schemes, typography, and user interfaces to build a visually appealing and user-friendly website. The goal is to ensure that visitors to your site have a seamless and enjoyable shopping experience. Yet eCommerce website design services are about more than just aesthetics. They also integrate essential features like shopping carts, secure payment gateways, and product catalogs. For this reason, these services help optimize your website’s performance, ensuring fast loading times and mobile responsiveness. Importance of User-Friendly and Visually Appealing eCommerce Websites Such eCommerce websites are of paramount importance in the realm of B2C eCommerce for several reasons. Attract and Retain Users Firstly, these websites are powerful tools for engaging users effectively. More than half of surveyed users are unlikely to recommend a poorly designed website to others. It’s because the visual appeal captivates users and keeps them immersed in the online shopping experience. Further, the significance of user-friendly design extends to customer retention. A well-crafted user interface can enhance a website’s conversion rates, while a bad user experience drives away customers. This underscores the direct impact of design on a website’s ability to retain its audience. Contribute to Business Success What do you think when looking at the website design of Pacific Northweast X-Ray Inc. ? The website seemingly showcases what the company offers (X-Ray products) but the design doesn’t look so professional. The layout appears outdated with the background gradient, cluttered layout, inconsistent typography, and navigation issues. This doesn’t only encourage visitors to explore the site further but also makes them suspect about the company’s offerings. Moreover, this can reduce their engagement with the business and decrease a likelihood of conversion, thereby affecting their business success. Considering examples from renowned brands, you’ll better understand the importance of user-friendly and visually appealing design. For example, Spotify’s use of a clean black and white theme with vibrant images, while Apple’s classic black and light gray theme. Additionally, in the competitive landscape of B2C eCommerce, where customer interaction is paramount, integrating top-notch user experience is essential. So, incorporate eCommerce call center outsourcing to further enhance customer satisfaction and make your business stand out. Further, mobile phones dominated eCommerce website visits and online orders, with roughly 77% . That’s why you should consider responsive website design that can function well across platforms. This will enhance the overall user experience and contribute to the success of an eCommerce platform. Differences Between B2C and B2B eCommerce Website Design Now, let’s discover three key differences between B2C and B2B eCommerce website designs: 1. Customer Intent Customer intents, or underlying incentives behind purchase decisions of B2B and B2C shoppers, are different. B2B: The implementation of B2B eCommerce website design is to prioritize companies whose buying decisions need to satisfy a group of different people. This takes those buyers a long time to list more detailed requirements for product assessment and thoroughly research such inputs. That’s why B2B e-tailers target top-of-the-funnel and middle-of-the-funnel leads. Those portals then strive to turn those prospective visitors to customers by using outbound (phone consultations or media buys) and inbound (content or paid search) marketing strategies. B2C: Meanwhile, B2C purchasers act on feelings and personal demands. They revel in browsing around to compare product prices and features. Therefore, there will be a decrease in the average time for sales reps to approach customers. Also, the relationship with B2C vendors will be temporary when compared to B2B counterparts. It’s because B2C customer intent is driven by such cognitive motives as scarcity bias, promotions, social proof and more. That motivates B2C sites to adopt optimization tactics to boost conversion rates. Recommended reading: Web Design: What It Is and Why It Matters? 2. Purchase Process The B2B purchase activities involve multiple stakeholders from distinctive departments, buying units, and even end-users. The ultimate goal of businesses isn’t to produce immediate sales but rather to attract more leads. Therefore, respective eCommerce websites often embrace business-oriented content, marketing assets (e.g. videos, emails, etc.), and interactive tools to specify how products and services tally with such a clientele’s requirements. By contrast, the B2C eCommerce website design facilitates product exploration and a sense of urgency among individual customers. They may either snap up products believed as good deals or snatch something highly recommended by previous shoppers. 3. User Experience Both B2C and B2B trading platforms want to maximize user experience (UX). But this trait varies depending on the mentioned customer intent and buying procedure. Both types of sites work on five different UX specifications: B2B eCommerce website design should accompany more informative, diverse content to support a longer-term purchase process. The B2B pricing mechanism is more complicated on the grounds of product customization, diversity, and sheer volumes. Also, B2B products can be negotiated for favorable discounts. B2B content must be tailored to decision-makers and end-users. Information and regulatory requirements of B2B products must be clear enough so that purchasers can determine whether those goods are compatible with their existing workflows and systems. B2B e-tailers serve different business clients in terms of industry, scale, and operational budget. Thus, B2B site navigation must be based on audience segmentation. Our eCommerce Web Design Process Every store we build follows a structured path from strategy through launch. Strategy & Discover UX Planning UI & Creative Design Responsive Development Quality Assurance Launch & Optimization Strategy & Discover We start by learning your business. What you sell, who buys it, what’s working and what isn’t. We define goals, identify your competitive edge and determine which eCommerce platform fits what you’re trying to build. Everything our eCommerce web design company does after this point is based on what we figure out in this phase. UX Planning Navigation gets mapped before anyone opens a design tool. Audience research shapes detailed wireframes, user flow and sitemap structures for every key page, including multi-language, multi-currency or regional setup if your store needs it. This is where structure gets right, before design and development build on top of it. UI & Creative Design Some stores need a fully custom interface. Others work better with a tailored theme. We figure out which approach fits your project and budget, then build out every screen with interactions placed where they help people buy. Responsive Development The approved design becomes a working store, not a static file. Custom functionality gets built the same way, all under one roof. Quality Assurance Nothing goes live until we’ve gone through the entire store ourselves . We test across devices and browsers, running the checkout process multiple times and looking for anything that could get in a customer’s way. A broken button, a slow page, a discount code that throws an error. We catch it before your customers do. Launch & Optimization The store goes live once everything is signed off, with our team monitoring closely through the first few days after launch. After things settle, attention shifts to performance: what pages hold attention, where visitors leave, which products get clicks but not purchases. A launch isn’t the end of the project. It’s the point where we start using real data to keep improving the store. ECOMMERCE MAINTENANCE & SUPPORT Your Store. Always Up to Date. Always Running. New Features & Functionality New Features & Functionality Six months after launch, your business won’t look the same as it did on day one. You might need a new payment option, a different shipping setup or a feature your competitors just added. We build and plug in whatever your store needs as things evolve. Content & Seasonal Updates Content & Seasonal Updates Seasonal moments move fast, and a homepage that doesn’t keep up loses relevance just as fast. We take care of content swaps, layout changes and campaign pages so your store stays current at all times. We hired Digital Silk as an A-to-Z solution for our brand launch in the US market. We started with fitting the brand strategy to the US market. With the data that we collected, we sharpened the brand strategy, which helped us develop together the website and the marketing plan. eCommerce Design & Development FAQs How long do eCommerce projects take? It depends. A simple eCommerce store can launch in a few weeks. Larger stores with custom design, integrations, complex catalogs or regional setups usually take a few months. We look at the platform, product count, features, content and approvals before giving you a timeline, so you know what to expect. How do I choose an eCommerce platform for my business? We build on Shopify Plus, Adobe Commerce (Magento) and WooCommerce, which between them cover everything from a boutique store to an enterprise catalog with millions of SKUs. Shopify Plus is best for speed to market and low operational overhead. Adobe Commerce fits complex B2B rules, multi-store setups or heavy customization. WooCommerce makes sense when the store sits alongside a content-led WordPress site. We recommend based on your catalog, integrations and internal team, not on what we’d prefer to build. Can you integrate payment options? Yes. We can set up Stripe, PayPal, Authorize.net, local payment gateways or a mix of providers, depending on what your business needs. We also check the full payment process, including checkout, order confirmations, failed payments and transaction data. Can you migrate my store from another platform? Yes. We map and migrate customer accounts, order history, products and content, run the full migration in a staging environment first and reconcile record counts and totals against the old system before anything goes live. SEO is the part most migrations get wrong, so we plan 301 redirects for every URL and preserve metadata and structured data. Passwords usually can’t transfer between platforms for security reasons, so we plan a simple reset flow for customers. AI tools help us flag data anomalies at scale, followed by a manual review before sign-off. Do you offer ongoing support and maintenance after launch? Yes. If we host your store, it gets a warranty period right after launch to fix any bugs at no cost. Beyond that, most eCommerce clients stay on a retainer covering technical maintenance and security updates, hosting, conversion rate optimization, new features and seasonal campaigns, catalog and content management, and digital marketing. A store isn’t finished at launch. The testing and improvements after go-live are usually where the biggest revenue gains come from. Will my store be responsive on mobile? Yes, our experts design and test your store for phones, tablets and desktop screens. We pay close attention to load speed, button placement, product images, forms and checkout steps so the store is easy to use on smaller screens. Should we choose a headless or traditional eCommerce setup? For most businesses, traditional. Headless gives you excellent speed and flexibility across multiple channels, but it costs more to build, needs ongoing developer support for front-end changes and takes some control away from your marketing team. It makes sense when you sell across several channels, run a large catalog with demanding performance needs or have an in-house dev team. If you mainly run one storefront, a well-built traditional setup is faster to launch and cheaper to own. We give you a straight recommendation after reviewing your requirements. Can you integrate our ERP, CRM and inventory systems? Yes. Complex integrations are a core part of what we do. We build custom API connections that sync products, inventory, pricing, orders and customer records between your store and your ERP, CRM, PIM, WMS or accounting system, with error handling and monitoring, so a failed sync gets caught instead of silently corrupting data. Where we’ve built a secure connector before, we reuse it to cut development time. If your system has no modern API, we scope a middleware approach and are upfront about the effort involved. Do you use pre-built eCommerce themes? No. Every storefront is custom designed around your products and your customers’ buying journey, because that’s where conversion rate comes from. A theme is designed for the average of thousands of stores, not for yours. We speed up delivery by reusing proven components from our own library and by augmenting our dev teams with AI, but the design itself is bespoke. In our experience, the money saved on a theme gets lost many times over in conversions. How do you design product pages that convert? By removing doubt. A high-converting product page answers the questions a buyer would otherwise leave to research: clear pricing and availability, customer support, honest photography from the angles that matter, specifications where relevant, delivery and returns stated plainly, and real reviews. We give the buy box visual priority, keep the add-to-cart button visible as shoppers scroll and place trust signals where hesitation happens, not in the footer. Then we test layout, imagery, copy and CTAs, and let the data settle disagreements about taste. How do you reduce cart abandonment? Mostly by removing reasons to hesitate: guest checkout as standard, shipping costs and delivery dates shown early instead of at the final step, a visible progress indicator, minimal form fields with address autocomplete, all the payment methods your customers expect, including digital wallets, and trust signals right where payment details are entered. We then back it up with abandoned cart email flows and, where it fits, retargeting. How do you handle search and filtering for large catalogs? With dedicated search and filtering, not the platform default. For large catalogs, we implement search with typo tolerance, synonyms, autocomplete and merchandising rules, so you can promote the right products. Filtering is faceted and built on a clean product taxonomy, which means the product data has to be right first, so we often clean up attributes as part of the project. After launch, we review real search queries, because what customers type shows what’s missing from your catalog and categories. How do you test checkout before launch? Checkout gets the heaviest testing of anything we build. Each dev team has a dedicated QA member, and we run software-assisted tests across hundreds of scenarios plus manual testing. We check every payment method, including declines and failed transactions, tax and shipping calculations across regions, discount and gift card logic, guest and registered checkout, items going out of stock during checkout, order confirmation emails and the full flow on real mobile devices. We also place live test orders end to end, and our CTO signs off before deployment. How do you keep our store secure and PCI compliant? By keeping card data off your site entirely. Payments are handled by certified gateways and processors, so card details never touch your servers, which keeps your PCI scope at the simplest level. On top of that, we implement SSL across the site, a web application firewall and DDoS protection through Cloudflare, encryption in transit, role-based admin access with two-factor authentication, regular patching, malware monitoring and automated backups. PCI compliance is a shared responsibility: we build and maintain the technical side, and your internal processes and staff access matter too. We show you exactly where the lines are. What happens if our store gets a traffic spike, like on Black Friday? We plan for it before it happens. If you host with us, we load-test the infrastructure against your expected peak ahead of major sales events, scale server resources in advance and set up caching and CDN rules to absorb the traffic. Our DevOps team monitors server load during those events with automated alerts, and we follow a documented incident response process, backed by encrypted backups and a disaster recovery plan. For Black Friday, we agree on a readiness plan and a code freeze with you well in advance.
